findings.subject: Peñón de los Baños as a Pleistocene island and travertine burial setting
findings.assertion: During the Late Pleistocene the small volcano now called Peñón de los Baños stood as an island in Lake Texcoco; hot springs built a travertine platform around it, and several prehistoric human skeletons were later recovered embedded in or below that travertine (Peñón I 1884, Peñón II 1957, Peñón III 1959, Peñón IV 1962).
locators: LJMU paper, section 'Sitio Paleoindio Peñón de los Baños' (no page numbers)
findings.evidence_summary: Gonzalez & Huddart describe the island, the travertine and four reported skeletons; Serrano Sánchez et al. independently describe the site as a former islet yielding the Basin's most abundant prehistoric human remains.
scholarly_disagreements: Count of individuals differs: Gonzalez & Huddart list four finds (Peñón I–IV); Serrano Sánchez et al. 2021 report Peñón III plus five other adults (citing Jiménez et al. 2010).
related_existing_records: v85-source-014 (Carballal & Flores 1992, El Peñón de los Baños (Tepetzinco)) — canonical source tagged to place; no canonical finding on prehistory
findings.visitor_relevance: Explains how a rocky rise inside today's city was once an island; the later Mexica name Tepetzinco links to the existing canonical source v85-source-014. Present-day public access to the find spots is NOT verified.

findings.subject: Peñón III: oldest directly dated human in the Basin of Mexico
findings.assertion: The Peñón III skeleton, a woman estimated at about 25 years old and ~1.51 m tall, has a direct AMS radiocarbon date on the left humerus of 10,755 ± 75 14C BP (OxA-10112), calibrated to roughly 12,560–12,760 cal BP, making it the oldest directly dated human from the Basin of Mexico.
locators: Serrano Sánchez et al. 2021, p.222 (cal. 12 561–12 761 AP)
findings.evidence_summary: Two texts (one by the dating team, one by an independent UNAM team citing it) give the same 14C age; the original 2003 J. Human Evolution report was not examined.
scholarly_disagreements: Error term reported as ±75 in both examined texts; popular summaries give ±55 — treat ±55 as unverified.
The LJMU text also prints '12,755 ± 75 BP', an apparent typographic slip.
findings.corroboration_note: Serrano et al. cite rather than re-date; this is consistent reporting, not independent measurement.
findings.visitor_relevance: Anchor date for any 'first people in the valley' narrative; cranium described as dolichocephalic (cranial index 70.05), relevant to F04 contrast.

findings.subject: Directly vs indirectly dated early individuals of the Basin
findings.assertion: Besides Peñón III, the Basin's early human record includes Tlapacoya I (direct date 10,200 ± 65 14C BP, ~11,600–12,150 cal BP), three adults from Santa María Astahuacán (10,300 ± 600 BP), and skulls from Balderas in the Centro Histórico and from Chimalhuacán dated only indirectly to ~10,500 years through association with Upper Toluca Pumice ash; Tepexpan and San Vicente Chicoloapan are younger than 9,000 years.
locators: LJMU paper, sections Chimalhuacán / Metro Balderas
findings.evidence_summary: Serrano et al. tabulate the individuals and explicitly separate direct dates from indirect (tephra) ages; Gonzalez & Huddart call the Balderas find 'Metro Man', a skull embedded in volcanic ash.
scholarly_disagreements: Indirect tephra ages date the ash, not the individual; they should not be presented with the same certainty as direct dates.
findings.visitor_relevance: The Balderas find places Ice Age human remains under the modern Centro Histórico (find circumstances and exact spot not verified in examined texts).

findings.subject: Tláhuac Woman and early cranial diversity
findings.assertion: A nearly complete but fragmented skeleton found by chance in 1966 during construction in Tláhuac, and donated to IIA-UNAM only in 2013, is a young woman (19–24 years, ~154.5 cm) dated by bone collagen to 8330 ± 40 BP (9465–9260 cal BP); her broad skull (cranial index 80.3) resembles modern Native American populations rather than the long, narrow late-Pleistocene pattern of Peñón III.
geographic_locations: Tláhuac (former island between lakes Xochimilco and Chalco)
locators: pp.221–223 (discovery), p.225 (Beta-443781 date; CI 80.3), pp.228–231 (age, stature, PCA)
findings.evidence_summary: Peer-reviewed full text gives lab number, calibration and morphometric comparison; the original find context could not be recovered and reported associations (mammoth tusk, grinding stone) are uncertain.
scholarly_disagreements: Whether early craniofacial variation reflects multiple migrations or local diversification is unresolved (authors' own framing, p.222).
findings.visitor_relevance: Gives the southern lake district (Tláhuac/Xochimilco) a directly dated early-Holocene inhabitant; useful contrast with Peñón III.

findings.subject: Tepexpan 'Man': from Ice Age hunter to mid-Holocene burial
findings.assertion: The Tepexpan skeleton, found by Helmut de Terra in 1947 near the eastern shore of former Lake Texcoco, was long presented as a ≥10,000-year-old mammoth hunter because of stratigraphic association with mammoth finds; later conventional radiocarbon results of ~2,000 BP were judged contaminated, and a uranium-series date on the skeleton of 4700 ± 200 years indicates a mid-Holocene age.
findings.evidence_summary: The dating team's abstract gives the U-series age; the UNAM 2023 article independently reviews the full sequence of dates (3,800–4,430 on overlying roots; ~2,000 on bone; ~4,700 U-series; 10,000–12,000 from stratigraphy).
scholarly_disagreements: U-series ages on bone are often treated as minimum ages (LJMU text describes it as a minimum); exact age remains uncertain.
findings.corroboration_note: Rojas Chávez et al. 2023 (UNAM/INAH authors, different team) review the same dating history and reach a compatible mid-Holocene reading.
findings.visitor_relevance: Tepexpan has a site museum (named in INAH Boletín 31/2024 'Ruta del Mamut' proposal and in Rojas Chávez et al. as the home of Larrauri's painting); current opening status not verified.

findings.subject: Tepexpan sex identification and stratigraphy disputed from the start
findings.assertion: Even mid-twentieth-century specialists disputed the Tepexpan interpretation: José Luis Lorenzo called de Terra's stratigraphy incoherent, Pablo Martínez del Río asked whether the individual drowned rather than died hunting, Weidenreich doubted it was male and Santiago Genovés identified it as female, and Javier Romero noted the broad skull resembled later farming populations.
findings.evidence_summary: Article reviews the original debate with citations to each scholar; original publications by those scholars not examined.
findings.visitor_relevance: Shows a visitor that the famous 'Tepexpan Man' label itself encodes an outdated reading.

findings.subject: Environmental instability of the Texcoco shoreline at Tepexpan
findings.assertion: Sediments at Tepexpan, with AMS dates between about 19,110 and 612 14C BP, record repeated shifts between saline-alkaline and fresher lake water, aquatic versus terrestrial and C3 versus C4 vegetation, volcanic ash input and sediment reworking, which the authors argue strongly affected people living on the lake shore.
findings.evidence_summary: Abstract-level; proxy data and figures not examined.
related_existing_records: v89-source-002 (Ortega-Guerrero et al. 2022, Xochimilco lake stratigraphy) — comparable record for southern basin
findings.visitor_relevance: Background for why the lake that later supported Tenochtitlan was not a stable environment over the long term.

findings.subject: Santa Isabel Iztapan: the Basin's only direct stone-tool–mammoth association
findings.assertion: At Santa Isabel Iztapan (Atenco, north shore of Lake Texcoco) two mammoths were excavated about 250 m apart; under the ribs of the second, found in 1954 and recovered by Luis Aveleyra Arroyo de Anda and Manuel Maldonado Koerdell, lay three stone tools, which INAH describes as still the only direct association of lithic artifacts with megafauna in the region.
findings.period: Terminal Pleistocene–Early Holocene (date contested, see F10)
geographic_locations: Santa Isabel Iztapan/Ixtapan, San Salvador Atenco, Estado de México
findings.evidence_summary: INAH bulletin and a peer-reviewed UNAM article agree on the two mammoths and the 1954 tool association; the primary 1956 report was not read.
scholarly_disagreements: Discovery date of Iztapan I: Rojas Chávez et al. say found 1949, excavated from 1952; INAH Boletín 3 implies first find ~1952. Unresolved pending Lorenzo & Mirambell 1986 'Mamutes excavados'.
Rojas Chávez et al. report six lithic items with Iztapan I (incl. a projectile point and obsidian blades), so 'only direct association' likely refers to both Iztapan mammoths jointly.
findings.visitor_relevance: Tools held by the Museo Nacional de Antropología (both INAH bulletins); exact case/hall placement not verified.

findings.subject: Iztapan II tools reinterpreted as butchering knives
findings.assertion: A 2023 use-wear study of the three Iztapan II tools—a flint biface, a flint Lerma-type point and a dacite Angostura-type point, 6–8 cm long—found wear on both edges and faces and a crackled micropolish associated with cutting bone or very hard material, leading INAH/ENAH researchers to interpret them as knives used for cutting and defleshing rather than hunting points; possible organic (grease-like) residue on the Lerma point awaited further testing.
locators: Rojas Chávez et al. 2023, pp.70–71 (Martínez del Río's earlier butchering interpretation of Iztapan I tools)
findings.source_access_level: full_text_examined (press release); no peer-reviewed report located
findings.evidence_summary: Methods stated: metallographic microscopy at 200x, SEM residue check, comparison with ENAH experimental catalogue (IIA-UNAM lab, two weeks). No journal article was cited.
scholarly_disagreements: Use as knives does not settle hunting vs scavenging: the bulletin addresses tool function only.
Earlier butchering interpretation by Martínez del Río for Iztapan I is consistent but concerns different artifacts.
findings.visitor_relevance: Lets a museum visitor re-read objects long labeled as spear points.

findings.subject: Unstable chronology of Santa Isabel Iztapan
findings.assertion: Ages proposed for Santa Isabel Iztapan range from 10,500–20,000 radiocarbon years in early work to obsidian-hydration ages of about 6,200–8,100 BP, while INAH's 2023 statements place the tool users at least about 9,000 years ago and state that this dating is itself under review.
findings.evidence_summary: No examined source presents a modern direct date on the Iztapan II mammoth or associated organic material.
scholarly_disagreements: A conference paper by Gonzalez's group (LJMU QI manuscript, snippet only) notes Iztapan lacks fluted Clovis points and places it after the PWA tephra — not examined, recorded as lead.
findings.visitor_relevance: Any app text should avoid a single date for Iztapan.

findings.subject: Possible seasonal lakeshore camp at Santa Isabel Iztapan
findings.assertion: In 2022 an INAH–ENAH project reopened the exact spot of the 1954 find and, in a nearby test pit, recovered small burned fish-bone fragments with charcoal and obsidian microflakes; researchers proposed a seasonal open-air hunter-gatherer camp that used lake resources as well as megafauna, an interpretation they described as preliminary.
geographic_locations: Santa Isabel Iztapan, north shore of former Lake Texcoco
findings.evidence_summary: Bulletin reports the materials and the hypothesis; dating basis not specified; extensive excavation planned for 2023 (outcome not located).
findings.visitor_relevance: Shifts the picture from heroic mammoth hunts to mixed lakeshore foraging.

findings.subject: Tocuila mammoth bonebed: size and discovery
findings.assertion: The Tocuila site in San Miguel Tocuila (Texcoco), found by chance in 1996 during cistern digging, produced about 1,000 bone fragments—over 90% Columbian mammoth—from at least seven individuals in about 28 m² at roughly 3 m depth, together with horse, camel, bison and other fauna.
geographic_locations: San Miguel Tocuila, Texcoco, Estado de México
findings.evidence_summary: Peer-reviewed text gives MNI ≥7 with skull/mandible counts.
scholarly_disagreements: LJMU symposium paper gives 'at least five' mammoths; the 2014 peer-reviewed figure (≥7) is preferred.
findings.visitor_relevance: Context for mammoth exhibits in the northeastern basin.

findings.subject: Tocuila mammoths were already dead before the lahar buried them
findings.assertion: Gonzalez et al. argue that the Tocuila bones were carried in a single rapid lahar sourced mainly from Upper Toluca Pumice ash (no older than ~10,761–10,455 cal BC), but that direct dates on mammoth bone (11,335–11,041 and 11,154–10,820 cal BC) show the animals died before that flow, so the eruption is unlikely to have killed them.
findings.evidence_summary: Bone orientation shows SE→NW transport; tusks still attached suggest short transport.
scholarly_disagreements: Siebe et al. (1999) attributed the lahar to the older PWA (Popocatépetl) and allowed a ~1,000-year accumulation; Gonzalez et al. 2014 reject this (pp.223, 233, 235).
Authors leave open whether bones accumulated before or with the mudflow (p.235).
findings.visitor_relevance: Volcanoes visible from the city (Popocatépetl, Nevado de Toluca) shaped the Ice Age basin.

findings.subject: Possible human bone quarrying at Tocuila
findings.assertion: Earlier analysts (Arroyo-Cabrales, Johnson and colleagues, 2001) identified impact-fractured mammoth bone, a bone core with a prepared platform and a cortical flake at Tocuila, interpreting them as human quarrying of fresh bone; Gonzalez et al. 2014 accept that this would imply people killed or scavenged the mammoths before burial but do not test the claim themselves.
findings.evidence_summary: Secondary; 2001 primary analyses not examined.
scholarly_disagreements: Human vs natural fracture of bone is a standard taphonomic dispute; independent assessment not located.
findings.visitor_relevance: Use cautiously: 'possible' human use only.

findings.subject: Contested Younger Dryas 'airburst' layer at Tocuila
findings.assertion: Gonzalez et al. 2014 report a thin layer with magnetic microspherules, charcoal and reported nanodiamonds dated 10,878–10,707 cal BC, which they attribute to a Younger Dryas meteorite airburst; they themselves note that other researchers (Haynes 2008; Scott et al. 2010; Pinter et al. 2011) offer non-impact explanations for such markers, and the impact hypothesis remains contested.
findings.evidence_summary: Recorded so the app does not adopt it as fact; critics' papers not examined.
scholarly_disagreements: Younger Dryas impact hypothesis is disputed in the wider literature; do not present as established.
findings.visitor_relevance: Not suitable for visitor narrative except as an example of an open debate.

findings.subject: Megafauna disappear from the Basin after the Upper Toluca Pumice eruption
findings.assertion: Gonzalez and colleagues report that megafauna are present in Basin of Mexico deposits up to the Upper Toluca Pumice eruption and absent afterward, and they suggest the eruption and associated ashfall, together with Younger Dryas climate change and human predation, contributed to megafaunal loss.
findings.evidence_summary: Single research group's synthesis; causal weighting not quantified.
scholarly_disagreements: Causes of American megafaunal extinction (climate, human hunting, other) are widely debated; see dispute D2 for chronological tension with Santa Lucía/Tultepec claims.
findings.visitor_relevance: Frames why mammoth-era fossils cluster at the end of the Pleistocene.

findings.subject: Tultepec I and II: scale of the finds
findings.assertion: In Tultepec (San Antonio Xahuento, north of Mexico City), INAH salvage work recovered a single mammoth skeleton (Tultepec I, 2015–2016) and, at a planned landfill site (Tultepec II, from 2019), two large pits containing the bones of at least 14 mammoths plus a few horse and camel bones; INAH's 2024 statement gives about 1,500 recovered bones and dates the activity to 15,000–13,000 years ago without stating the dating method.
geographic_locations: San Antonio Xahuento, Tultepec, Estado de México
findings.evidence_summary: Bulletin: ~400 m³ excavated; ≥14 mammoths; ~1,500 bones.
scholarly_disagreements: 2019 press coverage reported 824 bones; the 2024 bulletin's ~1,500 likely reflects the total after later work (not confirmed).
findings.visitor_relevance: Museo del Mamut de Tultepec (Mudema) in the municipal Casa de Cultura was scheduled to reopen in the second half of 2024 with ~1,000 m² and two near-complete skeletons; current status not verified.

findings.subject: Tultepec 'mammoth traps': excavator's interpretation and its limits
findings.assertion: The excavator, Luis Córdoba Barradas, interprets the Tultepec II pits as human-dug traps in a planned line spaced 40–50 m apart, with partial and complete butchery, a ritual arrangement of vertebrae around a skull, and selective absence of left scapulae and sterna; INAH itself notes no hunters' remains or stone tools were found, so human agency is inferred from bone arrangement, and an outside paleontologist (A. N. Rountrey, University of Michigan) said experts awaited peer-reviewed evidence that humans dug the pits.
locators: Smithsonian Smart News (Nov 2019), Rountrey quotation via NYT
findings.evidence_summary: Claims summarized from INAH; critique attributed via secondary journalism (primary NYT not examined). No peer-reviewed site report located in this run; the excavator's book is a lead.
scholarly_disagreements: Human construction of pits vs natural depressions; hunting vs scavenging; ritual reading of bone arrangement.
findings.visitor_relevance: Museum displays may present the trap model as fact; app should label it the excavator's interpretation.

findings.subject: Basin of Mexico mammoths form a distinct genetic lineage
findings.assertion: A 2025 INAH–UNAM paleogenomic study of 83 Columbian mammoth molars (73 from Santa Lucía, 10 from Tultepec) reported that Basin of Mexico mammoths belong to a mitochondrial lineage distinct from those of the United States and Canada, with three distinct, contemporaneous sublineages toward the end of the Pleistocene (~12,700 years ago); it is the first ancient mammoth DNA recovered from tropical latitudes.
geographic_locations: Santa Lucía / Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA), Zumpango
findings.evidence_summary: Bulletin: dentine sampling; 77 libraries with DNA; work at Laboratorio de Paleogenómica, Juriquilla; material housed at Centro de Investigación Paleontológica Quinametzin.
scholarly_disagreements: Number of mitogenomes (61 in news reports) and radiocarbon ages of samples not verified from the article.
findings.visitor_relevance: Connects the AIFA's Quinametzin paleontological museum to a current scientific debate.

findings.subject: 'Yotzin', a possible preceramic man from Santa Lucía
findings.assertion: During AIFA salvage work at site M3 near Cerro Xóloc, INAH recovered about 80% of a flexed male skeleton (25–30 years, ~1.75 m) in the upper part of a Pleistocene marsh layer with megafauna about half a metre away and no associated artifacts; INAH's estimate of ~10,000 years rests on morphology and stratigraphic correlation, not a radiocarbon date, and would make it the first preceramic human found in the Basin since the Chimalhuacán skull of 1984.
findings.evidence_summary: Bulletin explicitly states dating is pending and the age presumptive.
scholarly_disagreements: Age unconfirmed; do not present as Pleistocene.
findings.visitor_relevance: Hold for app use until a direct date is published.

findings.subject: First lakeshore settlements formed during a dry, cold interval
findings.assertion: A 2025 paleoenvironmental study of a trench at Tulyehualco, near the Zohapilco and Atlapulco sites, found that lake levels fell during the early Holocene and that dry-land conditions prevailed during the 8,200-year cold event—exactly when, by earlier archaeological dating, Zohapilco and Atlapulco were first occupied (~8,000–7,500 cal BP); wetter conditions returned ~7,500–6,500 cal BP.
findings.evidence_summary: Chronology from five bulk-sediment 14C dates and two tephras; the record is discontinuous; settlement dates are borrowed from earlier archaeology, not this core.
scholarly_disagreements: Unusually high charcoal from the mid-Archaic may reflect human burning, but volcanic causes are not excluded (authors).
related_existing_records: v89-source-002 (Ortega-Guerrero et al. 2022) — Xochimilco lake stratigraphy
findings.visitor_relevance: Xochimilco's watery landscape has a 8,000-year human history before chinampas.

findings.subject: Maize, beans and tubers ground at San Gregorio Atlapulco
findings.assertion: Starch and use-wear analysis of grinding stones excavated in 2013–2015 from the main domestic area of San Gregorio Atlapulco—once an islet in Lake Xochimilco, occupied in the transition to the first villages (6000–3500 BCE)—identified residues of sweet potato, common bean, maize, Physalis, chile and yam; the researchers describe a diet based mainly on gathered plants and lake resources, supplemented by domesticates such as maize.
findings.evidence_summary: Bulletin does not state number of tools, direct dates on residues, or which taxa are domesticated besides maize.
scholarly_disagreements: Paleoenvironmental core near the site shows Zea pollen only ~1,000 BP (Caballero et al. 2025), so early maize use here rests on residues, not pollen; see dispute D4.
related_existing_records: v91-claim-004 (canonical claim on San Gregorio Atlapulco ejido land limiting a different rescue excavation) — same place, different topic; not a duplicate
xochimilco area canonical gaps list 'Full 2025 household article and excavation tables' — possibly related but different study; check identity
findings.visitor_relevance: Direct link from Xochimilco's present to the Basin's earliest farmers; San Gregorio Atlapulco is a real place in the Xochimilco alcaldía (site visibility not verified).

findings.subject: Niederberger's Playa and Zohapilco phases: dates vary by source
findings.assertion: Christine Niederberger's excavations at Zohapilco (Tlapacoya, Lake Chalco), published 1976, defined preceramic Playa and Zohapilco phases that remain the framework for Archaic sedentism in the southern Basin, but recent sources give different starting dates (e.g., INAH 2025: Playa c.6500 BCE, Zohapilco c.3500 BCE; Caballero et al. 2025: Playa I c.8,000–7,500 cal BP).
findings.evidence_summary: Niederberger 1976 not examined (lead); difference may reflect calibrated vs uncalibrated dating.
findings.visitor_relevance: Needed before any app timeline labels 'first villages'.

findings.subject: The Museo Nacional de Antropología mammoth-hunt diorama as a historical artifact
findings.assertion: The mammoth-hunting diorama by sculptor Carmen Carrillo de Antúnez, inaugurated in September 1964 in the Museo Nacional de Antropología's 'Orígenes' hall (now 'Poblamiento de América'), was based on Iker Larrauri's painting for the Tepexpan museum, which followed Luis Aveleyra's dramatic 1959 narrative; Lorenzo criticized the scene as unsupported, the 2000 restructuring trimmed it and removed its backdrop, and a 2023 UNAM study proposes pairing it with new dioramas emphasizing mammoths as a resource rather than specialized hunting.
findings.evidence_summary: Lead author is identified elsewhere as curator-researcher of the Sala Poblamiento de América; article's conclusion not examined.
scholarly_disagreements: Whether Basin peoples specialized in mammoth hunting is the core dispute (see D1).
findings.visitor_relevance: HIGH: a visitor to the MNA's first hall can see the diorama and read it as a 1960s interpretation. Current display state should be field-verified.

disputes.topic: Did early Basin peoples hunt mammoths or mainly butcher/scavenge them?
positions: Excavator at Tultepec: human-dug trap line, organized hunting (INAH Boletín 31/2024).
Use-wear on Iztapan II tools: cutting/defleshing knives, not hunting points (INAH Boletín 364/2023) — function only, not acquisition.
UNAM museological review: emphasizes mammoth as resource over specialized hunting; weak ethnographic analogies (Rojas Chávez et al. 2023, pp.8, 14, 26).
Outside caution: awaiting peer-reviewed evidence for human-built pits (Rountrey via Smithsonian 2019).
disputes.evidence_status: No examined peer-reviewed site report for Tultepec; Iztapan tool study reported only by press release.

disputes.topic: A post-eruption gap in the human record?
positions: Gonzalez & Huddart: after the UTP eruption a hiatus of several millennia precedes reappearance of human skeletons (~4,500 yrs, Chicoloapan) (LJMU paper).

Counter-evidence in examined sources: Tláhuac Woman 9465–9260 cal BP (Serrano et al. 2021); Iztapan camp ~9,000 yrs (INAH 2023, provisional); Zohapilco/Atlapulco settlement ~8,000–7,500 cal BP (Caballero et al. 2025).
disputes.evidence_status: Synthesis by this research run; the gap claim may refer to skeletons with a specific dating method—needs checking against the LJMU paper's full context and later publications.

disputes.topic: Younger Dryas airburst layer at Tocuila
positions: Gonzalez et al. 2014: impact airburst markers.
Haynes 2008; Scott et al. 2010; Pinter et al. 2011 (cited by Gonzalez et al.): non-impact explanations.
disputes.evidence_status: Critics not examined; treat impact as contested minority hypothesis.

disputes.topic: When did maize enter Basin diets?
positions: Residues on Atlapulco grinding stones include maize, 6000–3500 BCE (INAH Boletín 22/2025).
Tulyehualco core shows Zea pollen only ~1,000 BP; does not date early maize (Caballero et al. 2025).
disputes.evidence_status: Not contradictory (residue vs local pollen production) but must not be conflated; JAS:Reports article not examined.

positions: Lorenzo & Mirambell (1986) reported hearths and an obsidian blade in >20,000-year contexts (per secondary sources only).
